_meta.descricao: The main Catholic pilgrimage shrines and basilicas in the world, from the Vatican to Aparecida.
_meta.aviso: This is not a complete list of the thousands of existing Catholic shrines; it covers some of the most visited and historically significant ones.

itens.titulo: Saint Peter's Basilica
itens.resumo: The principal church of Catholic Christendom, built over the traditional tomb of Saint Peter in the Vatican.
itens.corpo:
The first Basilica of Saint Peter was built between about 319 and 329 by order of the Emperor Constantine, on the Vatican, a hill on the right bank of the Tiber where Nero's circus had stood and where the oldest tradition places the martyrdom and burial of the Apostle Peter, crucified upside down around the year 64 or 67. The builders faced a considerable engineering challenge — part of the hillside had to be excavated and filled in, and a pre-existing pagan Roman cemetery had to be leveled — precisely so that the altar of the new church would be positioned directly over the venerated tomb of the Apostle, a sign that the location of the sepulcher, and not architectural convenience, dictated the entire plan of the building.

Fifteen centuries later, the old Constantinian basilica was in an advanced state of structural deterioration, and Pope Julius II decided in 1506 to demolish it and rebuild it completely, laying the foundation stone of a project entrusted to the architect Donato Bramante, who conceived a Greek-cross plan crowned by an immense dome. The work, which would extend over more than a century under twelve different popes, passed through successive architects — Raphael, Fra Giocondo, Antonio da Sangallo the Younger — until, in 1547, at the age of 71, Michelangelo took charge of the works, simplified the design back to Bramante's centralized plan, and redesigned the dome that would become the most recognizable symbol of Rome; he died in 1564 without seeing it completed, a task that fell to Giacomo della Porta and Domenico Fontana, who finished it in 1590. Carlo Maderno later extended the nave into the shape of a Latin cross and built the present façade, bringing the construction to a close in 1626 — exactly 1,300 years after the dedication of the original basilica.

Between 1656 and 1667, Gian Lorenzo Bernini completed the ensemble with the monumental elliptical colonnade of Saint Peter's Square, conceived as the "motherly arms of the Church" welcoming the faithful, the bronze baldachin over the high altar — part of the metal, according to a disputed tradition, taken from the portico of the Pantheon — and the Chair of Saint Peter in the apse. The basilica also houses Michelangelo's "Pietà" (1499), the only work the artist signed, sculpted when he was only 24 years old.

The archaeological confirmation of the tradition concerning Peter's tomb came only in the twentieth century: beginning in 1939, Pope Pius XII authorized excavations beneath the basilica that revealed a Roman necropolis from the first to the fourth centuries, with a small second-century monument (the "trophy of Gaius") erected exactly at the spot indicated by tradition as the burial place of the Apostle. In 1968, Pope Paul VI announced that bones found beside this monument were, with reasonable probability, attributable to Peter.

The largest church in the Catholic world by interior area and one of the four major papal basilicas of Rome, Saint Peter's is today the setting for the Pope's principal celebrations — canonizations, episcopal ordinations, the Christmas Mass, and the "urbi et orbi" blessing — and for the presentation of each new pontiff on the central loggia of the façade after his election in the Vatican.
itens.ano: Constantinian basilica c. 319-329; current basilica rebuilt between 1506 and 1626

itens.titulo: Basilica of Saint John Lateran
itens.resumo: The Pope's cathedral as Bishop of Rome, the oldest of the four major papal basilicas.
itens.corpo:
After defeating Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312, Emperor Constantine confiscated the lands of the Roman Laterani family and donated them to Pope Miltiades so that the first great public Christian basilica of Rome might be built there, initially dedicated to the Savior and inaugurated around 324 — thus older than Saint Peter's Basilica itself, and the episcopal see of Rome even before the Vatican became the center of Catholicism. For this reason the inscription on the façade proclaims it "mother and head of all the churches of the city and of the world" (omnium urbis et orbis ecclesiarum mater et caput): technically, it is there, and not at Saint Peter's, that the true cathedra of the Bishop of Rome is found.

Over fifteen centuries, the building suffered and survived successive catastrophes: an earthquake nearly destroyed it in 897, and two great fires, in 1308 and 1361, required extensive reconstructions paid for by the popes then residing in Avignon, despite the distance. In the seventeenth century, Francesco Borromini radically remodeled the interior at the request of Pope Innocent X, and in 1735 Pope Clement XII commissioned Alessandro Galilei to build the monumental Baroque travertine façade that stands today, crowned by fifteen colossal statues of Christ and of saints who founded religious orders.

Because of its institutional centrality, the basilica hosted five of the Church's ecumenical councils, the so-called Lateran Councils (1123, 1139, 1179, 1215 and 1512-1517) — the fourth of them, in 1215, among the most decisive of the Middle Ages, defined the doctrine of Eucharistic transubstantiation and established the obligation of annual confession and Paschal communion for every member of the faithful.

Beside the basilica stands the Holy Stairs (Scala Santa), traditionally identified with the steps of the praetorium of Pontius Pilate in Jerusalem, which Jesus is said to have climbed during his Passion and which Saint Helena, mother of Constantine, is said to have brought to Rome; pilgrims still climb its 28 steps on their knees today, as a sign of penance. At the top of the stairs is the chapel of the Sancta Sanctorum, the former private chapel of the popes, which houses the icon of the "Acheiropoieton," an image of Christ traditionally held to be "not made by human hands."

The Lateran complex — basilica, octagonal baptistery from the fourth century (one of the oldest still in use) and the former Lateran Palace — was the official residence of the popes for almost a thousand years, until the move to Avignon in the fourteenth century and, afterward, to the Vatican. It was also in the Lateran Palace that, in 1929, Cardinal Pietro Gasparri and Benito Mussolini signed the Lateran Pacts, which put an end to the "Roman Question," created the Vatican City State and granted the basilica and other ecclesiastical buildings in Rome the status of extraterritoriality.

itens.ano: original basilica inaugurated c. 324; current façade from 1735

itens.titulo: Basilica of Saint Mary Major
itens.resumo: The largest basilica dedicated to Mary in Rome, built after the Council of Ephesus (431), which defined her as "Mother of God."
itens.corpo:
According to tradition, a Roman patrician named John and his wife, a wealthy couple without children, promised to leave their entire fortune to build a church in honor of Mary; on the night of August 4 to 5, 358, Our Lady is said to have appeared in a dream both to John and to Pope Liberius, asking them to build the temple exactly where snow would fall the following morning. However strange it seemed in the height of the Roman summer, snow did in fact cover the summit of the Esquiline Hill that morning, and Pope Liberius himself is said to have traced the outline of the future church on the snow with a hoe — an episode celebrated every year, on August 5, with a shower of white petals released from the basilica's ceiling during Mass, in memory of the "legend of the snow."

The church seen today, however, was built somewhat later: it was erected under Pope Sixtus III, between 432 and 440, shortly after the Council of Ephesus (431) solemnly proclaimed Mary "Theotokos," Mother of God — thus becoming the first church in Rome explicitly dedicated to Mary under this newly defined dogmatic title. From the time of Sixtus III, the mosaics of the triumphal arch and the nave survive to this day, among the oldest and best-preserved mosaic cycles in the city, narrating episodes from the Old Testament and the infancy of Jesus.

The basilica also houses the icon "Salus Populi Romani" ("Protectress of the Roman People"), a Byzantine-style painting which tradition — without secure historical confirmation — attributes to the evangelist Luke; venerated for centuries as the protector of Rome, it was carried in procession through the city in 590 by Pope Gregory the Great to ask for an end to a plague, and became, more recently, an image of personal devotion for Pope Francis, who visited the chapel where it is kept before and after each international trip of his pontificate. Beneath the high altar, the Crypt of the Nativity also holds a reliquary with fragments of wood traditionally identified with the manger of Bethlehem.

Because of his lifelong bond with this Marian devotion, Pope Francis, who died on April 21, 2025, chose to break with the custom of recent popes — buried in the Vatican grottoes of Saint Peter's — and to be buried in Saint Mary Major, becoming the first pontiff buried outside the Vatican in more than a hundred years. His tomb, in a simple niche between the Pauline Chapel and the Sforza Chapel, is a slab of slate from the Italian region of Liguria — the land of his grandparents — with the single inscription "Franciscus" and a reproduction of his pectoral cross.

itens.titulo: Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls
itens.resumo: Built over the traditional tomb of Saint Paul the Apostle, the fourth of the major papal basilicas of Rome.
itens.corpo:
The Apostle Paul, according to tradition, was beheaded in Rome around the years 64-67, during the persecution of Nero, and buried in a plot of land along the Via Ostiense, outside the perimeter of the city walls. Over this site, venerated ever since, Constantine ordered the building of a first, modest basilica, which was enlarged over the course of the fourth century by the emperors Valentinian II, Theodosius I, Arcadius and Honorius until it became one of the largest Christian churches then in existence — a construction which, because it closely followed the orientation of the apostolic tomb and of the roads and Tiber embankments already present on the site, had to resolve structural and alignment challenges that were unusual for the time.

Unlike the old Basilica of Saint Peter, demolished during the Renaissance to make way for the present church, Saint Paul Outside the Walls kept its late-antique plan and structure practically intact for more than 1,400 years, becoming the most faithful architectural witness to what the great Constantinian basilicas of Rome must have been — until the night of July 15 to 16, 1823, when a fire, caused by the negligence of a workman who was repairing the lead covering of the roof, destroyed the building almost completely, along with a good part of its collection of early Christian, Byzantine, Renaissance and Baroque art. According to a popular account, still repeated today but whose truthfulness is disputed by historians, the cardinals concealed news of the tragedy from Pope Pius VII, who was then dying, so as not to shorten his last days.

The reconstruction, which sought to reproduce as faithfully as possible the plan and decoration that existed before the fire, received donations from sovereigns and Catholic communities all over the world — from the viceroy of Egypt to the emperor of Brazil — a testimony to the universal prestige of the shrine; the new basilica was consecrated in 1840 by Pope Gregory XVI, and the great entrance quadriporticus would only be completed in 1928.

One of the best-known features of the interior is the unbroken series of mosaic medallions with the portrait of every pope in history, a tradition said to go back to Pope Leo the Great in the fifth century, and which had to be entirely redone after the fire of 1823; a medieval legend, still repeated today by tour guides, claims that the world will end when there is no more room in the basilica for the portrait of a new pope. The basilica also keeps ancient Byzantine bronze doors from the eleventh century, donated by a wealthy merchant of Amalfi and cast by craftsmen of Constantinople, damaged but preserved after the fire.

Because of its dedication to the "Apostle of the Gentiles," the basilica is also the traditional setting for ecumenical celebrations, among them the closing ceremony of the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, celebrated every year on January 25, the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul.
itens.ano: original basilica from the fourth century; rebuilt after the fire of 1823 and consecrated in 1840

itens.titulo: Sanctuary of Fatima
itens.resumo: One of the largest Marian shrines in the world, built on the site of the 1917 apparitions in Portugal.
itens.corpo:
On May 13, 1917, three children who were tending sheep at the Cova da Iria, near Fatima — Lúcia de Jesus dos Santos, aged 10, and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, aged 9 and 7 — claimed to have seen a "Lady brighter than the sun," holding a white rosary. According to the account of the shepherd children, the apparition recurred on the 13th of each month between May and October of that year — with the exception of August, when the children, detained by the local administrator of the municipality, who was hostile to the phenomenon at the time, were only able to see the Lady on August 19, at a different place.

The messages attributed to the apparition insisted on the daily praying of the rosary for peace and for the end of the First World War, on penance and on the conversion of sinners, and included what became known as the "three secrets of Fatima": a vision of hell, a prophecy associated with the Second World War and the spread of the errors of Russia, and a third secret, of a more enigmatic content, made public by the Holy See only in 2000 and interpreted by John Paul II as related to the assassination attempt he suffered in 1981. In October, the Lady identified herself as "Our Lady of the Rosary."

The most famous event took place on October 13, 1917, the so-called "Miracle of the Sun": before a crowd estimated at between 30,000 and 100,000 people — which included skeptics, journalists and curious onlookers drawn by the promise, announced in advance, of a visible sign — witnesses reported seeing the sun spin, tremble and change color in the sky, a phenomenon recorded even by the non-confessional press of the time.

The fate of the three shepherd children deeply marked later devotion: Francisco died in 1919 and Jacinta in 1920, both victims of the Spanish flu pandemic while still children; Lúcia became a Carmelite nun, living under the name Sister Lúcia of Jesus and of the Immaculate Heart until her death in 2005, at the age of 97. Francisco and Jacinta were canonized by Francis in 2017, on the centenary of the apparitions, becoming the youngest non-martyr saints in the history of the Church; the cause for Lúcia's canonization is underway.

A small chapel, the Little Chapel of the Apparitions, was built in 1919 exactly over the site of the visions; around it, over the following decades, the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary grew, elevated to a minor basilica by Pope Pius XII in 1954, and later the modern and spacious Basilica of the Most Holy Trinity, inaugurated for the ninetieth anniversary of the apparitions, in 2007. Lúcia, Francisco and Jacinta are now buried in the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary. The sanctuary has received visits from several popes — Paul VI in 1967, John Paul II three times (the 1982 visit marked by his personal thanksgiving to Our Lady for having survived the assassination attempt of the previous year, whose bullet was set into the crown of the statue), Benedict XVI in 2010 and Francis in 2017 — and today receives millions of pilgrims every year, especially on the monthly anniversaries of May 13 and October 13.
itens.ano: 1917 (apparitions); Little Chapel of the Apparitions in 1919; minor basilica in 1954

itens.titulo: Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe
itens.resumo: The most visited Marian shrine in the world, built on the site of the apparition to Saint Juan Diego in 1531.
itens.corpo:
In December 1531, ten years after the Spanish conquest of Tenochtitlan, the converted indigenous man Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin, on his way to Mass, is said to have encountered on the hill of Tepeyac — a former site of worship of the Aztec deity Tonantzin — a young lady who asked him to request of Bishop Juan de Zumárraga the building of a church there. Faced with the bishop's skepticism, who demanded a sign, the lady instructed Juan Diego, on December 12, to gather Castilian roses — a bloom impossible on that arid hill in the middle of the Mexican winter — and carry them in his tilma (a cloak of agave fiber) to Zumárraga; when he opened the cloak before the bishop, the flowers fell and the image of the Virgin appeared imprinted on the fabric itself.

The image — which depicts a Virgin of mestizo features, standing on a crescent moon, surrounded by rays of the sun, with stars on her mantle and an angel at her feet — combines, according to scholars, both Christian symbolism (the "woman clothed with the sun" of the Apocalypse) and recognizable elements of the Nahua indigenous worldview, which is said to have greatly facilitated the evangelization and the mass conversions of the native population of central Mexico in the years following the event.

The tilma, made of plant fiber, a material that would normally deteriorate within a few decades, remains preserved almost five hundred years later, having been exposed without special protection for a good part of that time; throughout the twentieth century, various technical studies — among them the digital analysis of the eyes of the image carried out by the engineer José Aste Tonsmann, who claims to have identified multiple figures reflected in the pupils — have been cited by devotees as evidence of unexplained anomalies, although such interpretations are disputed by skeptics and are not a matter of dogmatic teaching by the Church.

Juan Diego was canonized on July 31, 2002, by Pope John Paul II, becoming the first indigenous saint of the Americas. Our Lady of Guadalupe was declared patroness of the Americas by Pope Pius XII in 1945.

The first Guadalupan hermitage of the sixteenth century was replaced by a large Baroque basilica built between 1695 and 1709, which over the following centuries sank unevenly into the unstable lakebed soil of Mexico City, to the point of becoming structurally dangerous and visibly tilted. A new circular basilica, designed by the architect Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, was then built between 1974 and 1976 and inaugurated on October 12, 1976, with a capacity of more than ten thousand people and moving walkways that allow pilgrims to contemplate the tilma without interrupting the flow of visitors — a necessary solution given the massive influx to the most visited shrine in the Catholic world, with estimates of up to twenty million pilgrims per year, especially around the feast of December 12.

itens.titulo: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes
itens.resumo: One of the greatest centers of pilgrimage and reported healings in the Catholic world, in the south of France.
itens.corpo:
Bernadette Soubirous was born in 1844 in Lourdes into a very poor family, which at that time was living in a disused former prison cell, the "cachot." On February 11, 1858, at the age of 14, Bernadette, who was gathering firewood on the banks of the Gave River with her sister and a friend, saw in a hollow of the rock of the Massabielle grotto a young lady dressed in white, with a blue sash at her waist, golden roses at her feet and a rosary in her hands.

The apparition was repeated eighteen times between February and July of that year. On one occasion, the lady asked Bernadette to dig in the ground of the grotto; from that spot a trickle of muddy water sprang up, which soon became a perennial spring, today associated with thousands of reports of physical and spiritual healing — of which the International Medical Bureau of Lourdes, after rigorous scientific and canonical evaluation over more than a century, has formally recognized only about seventy as inexplicable by medicine. On March 25, the feast of the Annunciation, the lady revealed her name in the local Occitan dialect: "Que soy era Immaculada Concepciou" ("I am the Immaculate Conception") — a phrase of theological weight that the young girl, with no education whatsoever, could hardly have known on her own, since the dogma of the Immaculate Conception had been proclaimed by Pius IX only four years earlier, in 1854.

The local civil authorities reacted with suspicion — the police commissioner Jacomet even interrogated Bernadette in an attempt to make her contradict herself — and the ecclesiastical hierarchy itself initially adopted a cautious stance. The Bishop of Tarbes appointed a canonical commission that investigated the case for four years before declaring, in 1862, that the apparitions deserved credence and officially authorizing the cult of Our Lady of Lourdes.

Bernadette entered the congregation of the Sisters of Charity of Nevers in 1866, at the age of 22, where she lived discreetly and in suffering, aggravated by chronic asthma and tuberculosis of the bone, until her death in 1879, at the age of 35. Her body was exhumed three times during the canonization process and found in a remarkable state of preservation — today displayed in a glass reliquary in Nevers, with a wax mask covering the face and hands, according to the clarification given by the Church itself regarding the state of the relic. She was canonized in 1933 by Pope Pius XI.

Around the grotto, successive basilicas were built over the decades: the Upper Basilica of the Immaculate Conception, consecrated in 1876; the Basilica of the Rosary, from 1889; and the monumental Underground Basilica of Saint Pius X, inaugurated in 1958, with a capacity for 25,000 people, one of the largest ecclesiastical structures in the world. The sanctuary today receives between four and six million pilgrims a year — many of them sick or disabled, seeking the pools of spring water — and every night it is the scene of Marian candlelight processions that have become famous throughout the Catholic world. The rigorous medical-theological verification methodology developed at Lourdes has since become a reference model for the analysis of healings attributed to supernatural intercession at other sanctuaries.

itens.titulo: National Shrine of Aparecida
itens.resumo: The largest Marian shrine in the world, devoted to Our Lady of Aparecida, Patroness of Brazil, whose image was found by fishermen in the Paraíba River in 1717.
itens.corpo:
The National Shrine of Aparecida, in Aparecida (SP), originates in the image of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception found in October 1717 in the Paraíba do Sul River by the fishermen Domingos Garcia, João Alves and Filipe Pedroso. According to the accounts, the body of the image was pulled out first, without the head, and the head appeared shortly afterward, fitting perfectly. The fishermen had been charged by the Municipal Council of Guaratinguetá with obtaining fish for the banquet offered to Dom Pedro de Almeida e Portugal, Count of Assumar, governor of the captaincy of São Paulo and Minas Gerais, who was visiting the region between October 17 and 30 of that year. After the discovery, their nets are said to have filled with fish, an episode known as the Miraculous Catch.

Devotion grew around the small terracotta image, at first housed in an oratory and later in successive chapels. The image was solemnly crowned in 1904, in the name of Pope Pius X, by decree of the Holy See. On July 16, 1930, Pope Pius XI proclaimed Our Lady of Aparecida Queen and Patroness of Brazil. From 1894, the pastoral care and administration of the shrine were entrusted to the Redemptorist Missionaries.

In view of the steady growth in the number of pilgrims, construction of the so-called New Basilica began in 1955, conceived by the architect Benedito Calixto in the form of a Greek cross, 173 m long by 168 m wide, with naves 40 m high and a dome 70 m high. On July 4, 1980, during his first visit to Brazil, Pope John Paul II consecrated the church and conferred upon it the title of basilica; in the same year, Law No. 6,802 of June 30 established October 12 as a national holiday dedicated to the patroness. In 1983, the National Conference of Bishops of Brazil declared the church a National Shrine.

Among the visitors counted at the shrine are, besides John Paul II (1980), Pope Benedict XVI (2007, at the opening of the Fifth General Conference of the Latin American Episcopate, held in Aparecida) and Pope Francis (2013). The great influx of pilgrims is concentrated above all on the feast day of October 12.

itens.ano: 1717 (discovery of the image); current basilica inaugurated in stages starting in 1955

itens.titulo: Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela
itens.resumo: The final destination of the Camino de Santiago, built over the traditional tomb of the Apostle James the Greater, whose discovery in the 9th century gave rise to the Jacobean pilgrimage.
itens.corpo:
The Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, in Spanish Galicia, houses the tomb traditionally identified as that of Saint James the Greater, Apostle, and is the final destination of the "Camino de Santiago" (Way of Saint James), one of the oldest and most traveled pilgrimage routes in Christianity.

According to the tradition recorded in Galician sources and on the official Camino website, in the 9th century Bishop Theodemir of Iria Flavia identified a small shrine of Roman origin as the sepulcher of the Apostle. Following that discovery, King Alfonso II the Chaste had a modest church built over the earlier structure. The discovery also served purposes of political cohesion for the Asturian kingdom: at a time when Rome had lost prestige and Jerusalem remained inaccessible because it was under Muslim rule, Compostela was promoted as a new pilgrimage center of Western Christendom. The measure taken by Ordoño II in 915 — by which anyone who resided for forty days without being claimed as a serf became a free man with the right to live in the city — illustrates how the pilgrimage shaped the very urban formation of Compostela.

The increase in pilgrimages and the relative stability after the Arab attacks led to a new and great construction, begun in 1075, during the reign of Alfonso VI and under the direction of Bishop Diego Peláez. The Romanesque work continued during the archbishopric of Diego Gelmírez, who in 1120 obtained for the see of Compostela the dignity of a metropolitan church. The church is built of granite ashlar, with a Latin cross plan, an ambulatory at the head of the church, and a tribune running along the entire perimeter.

Among its façades, the Obradoiro, the work of Fernando Casas y Novoa (1738-1750), combines stone and glass and opens onto the square where pilgrims complete their journey. The historic center of the old city, with its cathedral, was inscribed by UNESCO on the World Heritage List in 1985. The pilgrimage is intensified in the Jacobean Holy Years, celebrated whenever the feast of Saint James, on July 25, falls on a Sunday.

itens.titulo: Divine Mercy Sanctuary (Kraków)
itens.resumo: Sanctuary in Kraków-Łagiewniki, beside the tomb of Saint Faustina Kowalska, the world's main center of devotion to the Divine Mercy.
itens.corpo:
The Divine Mercy Sanctuary (in Polish, Sanktuarium Bożego Miłosierdzia) is located in the Łagiewniki district, in the southern part of Kraków, Poland. The site belongs to the convent complex of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy, founded in 1862, whose neo-Gothic building was constructed between 1889 and 1891. Saint Maria Faustina Kowalska (1905-1938) lived and died there; according to her Diary, Jesus Christ entrusted to her the message of the Divine Mercy.

Faustina's remains were transferred to the convent church in 1966. In 1968, the then Cardinal Archbishop of Kraków, Karol Wojtyła, the future John Paul II, designated that church as a sanctuary because of the religious sister's relics. Since Faustina's beatification in 1993, her remains rest above the altar, beneath the image of the Merciful Jesus. In 1985, John Paul II called Łagiewniki the "capital of the devotion to the Divine Mercy."

The image venerated on the side altar of this sanctuary is the one by Adolf Hyła: the first version was blessed on March 7, 1943, and a second one, made for the niche above the side altar, was blessed on April 16, 1944, the first Sunday after Easter, by Father Józef Andrasz, Faustina's confessor in Kraków. This image should be distinguished from the first painting of the Merciful Jesus, executed in 1934 in Vilnius by the artist Eugeniusz Kazimirowski, under the direction of Faustina and her confessor, Blessed Michał Sopoćko — that original image is today in the Divine Mercy Sanctuary in Vilnius, Lithuania, and not in Kraków.

The present large basilica was built between 1999 and 2002, designed by the architect Witold Cęckiewicz and with a form evoking a boat, and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II on August 17, 2002. On that occasion the pontiff entrusted the world to the Divine Mercy. The church can hold about 5,000 people, and John Paul II visited the sanctuary in 1997 and 2002. The devotion to the Divine Mercy and the cult connected with Faustina were at one point the subject of a Notification of the Congregation of the Holy Office in 1959 (published in Acta Apostolicae Sedis), whose prohibitions were declared without effect by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith on April 15, 1978; Faustina was canonized by John Paul II on April 30, 2000, and in the same year the pontiff instituted for the whole Church the Feast of the Divine Mercy, on the Second Sunday of Easter.

itens.titulo: Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary (Convent of Santo Domingo, Buenos Aires)
itens.resumo: Former Dominican church and convent in the historic center of Buenos Aires, marked by the defense of the city against the British invasions and by the tomb of General Manuel Belgrano.
itens.corpo:
The Dominicans settled in the early eighteenth century on the city block in central Buenos Aires where their church and convent now stand; construction of the present building began in 1751 under a design by the architect Antonio Masella, was continued from 1762 by Francisco Álvarez and, from 1774, by Manuel Álvarez de Rocha, and the church was consecrated in 1783 — although the roofing and the left tower remained incomplete for decades. With a simple plan and three naves, the central nave covered by a barrel vault and a dome over the crossing, the church preserves the sober character typical of the colonial churches of the Río de la Plata.

The building was a direct stage of the British invasions of 1806 and 1807: during the Second Invasion, British troops entrenched themselves in the church's left tower, and the marks of gunfire and of a cannonball fired by the Buenos Aires defenders during the reconquest of the city remain visible to this day in the masonry of the tower. Tradition holds that Santiago de Liniers, commander of the reconquest, promised Friar Gregorio Torres that, if Our Lady of the Rosary granted him victory, he would donate to the church the flags taken from the British invaders; once the promise was fulfilled, the flags were delivered on August 24, 1806, and are still displayed today in the left side aisle, next to banners donated later by General Manuel Belgrano, from battles of the Argentine war of independence.

Belgrano himself — creator of the Argentine flag and a member of the Dominican Third Order — requested in his will to be buried in this church; his first tomb was modest, but in 1903 an imposing mausoleum, the work of the Italian sculptor Ettore Ximenes, was inaugurated in the atrium, and it became one of the most visited civic monuments in Buenos Aires. Raised to the dignity of a minor basilica in the twentieth century, the church remains today, at once, an active Dominican parish, a Marian shrine of the Rosary, and one of the historical landmarks most laden with patriotic symbolism in the Argentine capital, uniting Marian devotion and the memory of national independence.
itens.ano: construction begun in 1751; church consecrated in 1783

itens.titulo: Shrine of Jasna Góra (Częstochowa)
itens.resumo: Home of the icon of the Black Madonna of Częstochowa, the main center of Marian pilgrimage in Poland.
itens.corpo: Built on the hill of Jasna Góra, in the Polish city of Częstochowa, the shrine has housed since the fourteenth century the icon known as Our Lady of Częstochowa, the Black Madonna — an image which tradition attributes, without secure historical confirmation, to Saint Luke the Evangelist. The monastery, entrusted to the Pauline monks, withstood a Swedish siege in 1655, an episode that consolidated its image as a symbol of Polish Catholic identity. It receives millions of pilgrims every year, being one of the largest Marian shrines in Europe.

itens.titulo: Shrine of the Holy House of Loreto
itens.resumo: Italian basilica that houses the Holy House, traditionally venerated as the very house in Nazareth where the Holy Family lived.
itens.corpo: The Italian shrine of Loreto, in the Marche, was built around a small stone house that tradition, since the thirteenth century, identifies as the Holy House of Nazareth — the dwelling of the Holy Family, which is said to have been transported there (according to popular devotion, by angels; according to more recent historical research, possibly by crusaders or merchants). It has been the patroness of aviators since the twentieth century, by symbolic association with the legend of the aerial transport of the house.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Mroselli / Rabanus Flavus — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5
itens.ano: shrine built beginning in the fifteenth century

itens.titulo: Our Lady of Knock Shrine
itens.resumo: Ireland's principal Marian shrine, built on the site of a silent apparition witnessed by fifteen people in 1879.
itens.corpo: On August 21, 1879, in the small Irish village of Knock, fifteen witnesses claimed to have seen, on the outer wall of the local church, a silent apparition of Our Lady, Saint Joseph and Saint John the Evangelist, together with a lamb on an altar. Unlike other famous Marian apparitions, there was no spoken message and no single visionary — the event was investigated by ecclesiastical commissions in 1879 and 1936, which found the witnesses' testimonies satisfactory. The shrine became Ireland's principal center of Marian pilgrimage, visited by John Paul II in 1979 and by Francis in 2018.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Michael McLaughlin Photography — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

itens.titulo: Shrine of Saint Pio of Pietrelcina (San Giovanni Rotondo)
itens.resumo: One of the most visited shrines in Italy, built around the tomb and the convent where Padre Pio lived for decades.
itens.corpo: In San Giovanni Rotondo, in the region of Apulia (Italy), the shrine brings together the Capuchin convent where Saint Pio of Pietrelcina (Padre Pio) lived most of his religious life, the hospital he founded (Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza) and, since his canonization in 2002, the tomb that holds his remains. It has become one of the most sought-after pilgrimage destinations in Italy, alongside Rome and Assisi, attracting devotees drawn above all by his fame for the stigmata, mystical gifts and spiritual direction.

itens.titulo: Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi
itens.resumo: Italian basilica built over the tomb of Saint Francis, famous for Giotto's frescoes on the life of the saint.
itens.corpo: Built in Assisi, in Umbria (Italy), shortly after the canonization of Saint Francis in 1228, the basilica that bears his name is divided into two superimposed churches — the Lower Basilica, which houses the saint's tomb in a crypt, and the Upper Basilica, whose frescoes, attributed in part to Giotto, narrate episodes from the life of Francis and became a decisive reference for Western painting. It is one of the most visited pilgrimage destinations in Italy, especially among those who follow Franciscan spirituality.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Georges Jansoone — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.5

itens.titulo: Shrine of Our Lady of La Salette
itens.resumo: Shrine in the French Alps built on the site where, in 1846, two young shepherds claimed to have seen the Virgin Mary weeping, with an appeal to the conversion of the people.
itens.corpo:
On September 19, 1846, two shepherds from Corps, in the French region of Isère — Maximin Giraud, aged 11, and Mélanie Calvat, aged 14 — reported having seen, high in the Alps at an altitude of more than 1,800 meters (about 5,900 feet), a “beautiful lady” seated and weeping, who entrusted to them a long appeal to conversion and penance, addressed to “all her people.”

Pope Pius IX officially approved the cult of the apparition in 1851, and in 1879 Pope Leo XIII raised the shrine to the rank of minor basilica, also decreeing the canonical coronation of Our Lady of La Salette. The shrine, today entrusted to the Missionaries of Our Lady of La Salette — a congregation founded because of the event itself —, is the second most visited Marian pilgrimage destination in France, after Lourdes.

itens.titulo: Shrine of Our Lady of Walsingham
itens.resumo: Ancient English Marian shrine, traditionally linked to a vision in 1061, destroyed during the Reformation and re-established by Catholics in the twentieth century.
itens.corpo:
According to tradition, in 1061 the English noblewoman Richeldis de Faverches was carried in spirit to the house at Nazareth and was asked to build, in her village of Walsingham, a replica of that home of the Holy Family, the "Holy House." Over the course of the Middle Ages the site became one of the greatest pilgrimage destinations of Christendom, ranking alongside Jerusalem, Rome and Santiago de Compostela; King Henry VIII himself visited it as a pilgrim before, as head of the Church now separated from Rome, ordering its destruction in 1538.

The shrine lay in ruins for almost four centuries. In the early twentieth century it was restored, first by Anglicans and, from 1934, also by Catholics, who built a new National Shrine with a replica of the medieval image of Our Lady of Walsingham. Today it receives tens of thousands of pilgrims each year and is a symbol of Marian devotion in England.

itens.titulo: Basilica of Our Lady of Charity of El Cobre
itens.resumo: Cuban national shrine that houses the image of the country's patroness, found by three fishermen in the Bay of Nipe in 1612.
itens.corpo:
According to tradition, in 1612 three fishermen — the brothers Juan and Rodrigo de Hoyos and the enslaved boy Juan Moreno, known as “the three Juans” — found floating in the Bay of Nipe, in eastern Cuba, a small wooden image of Our Lady with the Child Jesus, bearing on its base the inscription “Yo soy la Virgen de la Caridad” (“I am the Virgin of Charity”). The image was taken to the mining town of El Cobre, where it is still venerated today.

In 1916 Pope Benedict XV proclaimed Our Lady of Charity of El Cobre patroness of Cuba, and in 1936 Pius XI presided over her canonical coronation. In 1977 Paul VI raised the shrine to the dignity of a minor basilica. The devotion, deeply rooted in Cuban identity, endured decades of communist rule and has been visited by three popes — John Paul II (1998), Benedict XVI (2012) and Francis (2015).

itens.titulo: Basilica of Our Lady of Luján
itens.resumo: Argentine national shrine built on the site where, according to tradition, an image of the Immaculate Conception refused to continue its journey in 1630, becoming the patroness of the country.
itens.corpo:
Tradition places the origin of the devotion in 1630, when a small terracotta image of the Immaculate Conception, brought from Brazil, was being transported by cart toward Santiago del Estero. On reaching the banks of the Luján River, the cargo simply could not be moved from the spot until the very box containing that image was removed — a sign interpreted as the Virgin's wish to remain there. Around the image, now known as Our Lady of Luján, one of the largest Marian shrines in South America took shape.

On May 8, 1887, Pope Leo XIII presided over the canonical coronation of the image, establishing her as patroness of Argentina — and, in time, of Uruguay and Paraguay as well. The neo-Gothic basilica that now houses the image, about 70 km from Buenos Aires, was officially recognized by the Holy See as a basilica in 1930 and receives millions of pilgrims every year, especially during the traditional Youth Pilgrimage on foot from Buenos Aires to Luján.

itens.titulo: Sanctuary of Bom Jesus do Monte
itens.resumo: Portuguese religious and landscape complex dedicated to the Good Jesus, famous for its Baroque staircase with fountains and chapels of the Way of the Cross, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
itens.corpo:
The devotion on Monte Espinho, on the outskirts of Braga, dates back to the 14th century, when a cross was erected there and, shortly afterward, a small hermitage dedicated to the Holy Cross. Over more than 600 years the site was expanded until it became one of the most notable European examples of a "sacred mount" — a tradition of sanctuaries that reproduce the episodes of the Way of the Cross in staircases and chapels, encouraged by the Church after the Council of Trent as a response to the Protestant Reformation.

The present church, one of the first Neoclassical buildings in Portugal, was designed by the architect Carlos Amarante at the request of the Archbishop of Braga, Dom Gaspar de Bragança, with construction taking place between 1784 and 1811. The famous monumental staircase, with its allegorical fountains of the five senses and the virtues, leads pilgrims up the hill to the church. Raised to the status of basilica in 2015, the sanctuary had its entire architectural and landscape complex recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.
itens.ano: begun in the 14th century; present church 1784-1811; basilica in 2015

itens.titulo: Shrine of Montserrat
itens.resumo: Catalan Benedictine monastery built on the jagged mountain of Montserrat, which houses the venerated Romanesque image of the Black Madonna (La Moreneta).
itens.corpo:
Nestled at an altitude of 720 meters on the distinctive mountain of Montserrat, the monastery of Santa Maria was founded in 1025 by Abbot Oliba on the site of an earlier hermitage donated by Wilfred the Hairy to the monastery of Ripoll. According to legend, the image of the Virgin had already been found by shepherds in a cave on the mountain in the year 880, guided by a mysterious light and song.

The venerated image, popularly known as “la Moreneta” because of its darkened color — attributed, according to recent studies, to the blackening caused by candle smoke over the centuries —, is a Romanesque carving in poplar wood from the 12th century, about 95 cm tall, depicting Mary enthroned with the Child. In 1881 Pope Leo XIII declared her patroness of the dioceses of Catalonia. Throughout the 17th and 18th centuries, the Escolania of Montserrat, one of the oldest music schools in Europe, established the monastery as an important cultural center, and today the shrine is one of the most visited pilgrimage and religious tourism destinations in Spain.

itens.titulo: Basilica of Our Lord of Bonfim
itens.resumo: A church in Bahia built in fulfillment of a vow made by a Portuguese captain in the 18th century, which became the foremost symbol of popular devotion and of Afro-Brazilian culture in Salvador.
itens.corpo:
The construction of the church dedicated to Our Lord Jesus of Bonfim resulted from a vow made by the Portuguese captain Theodósio Rodrigues de Faria, who brought from Lisbon, in 1745, an image of Christ crucified to be venerated in Salvador. The church was built between 1746 and 1754 on top of the hill of Itapagipe, and it received later additions to its Rococo façade and to its Neoclassical interior decoration throughout the 18th and 19th centuries.

In 1927 Pope Pius XI raised the church to the dignity of a basilica. The Feast of Our Lord of Bonfim, celebrated without interruption since 1745 with the traditional washing of the church steps by baianas dressed in traditional attire, has become one of the greatest symbols of the syncretism between popular Catholicism and Afro-Brazilian traditions, and the church is also famous for its room of miracles, where the faithful leave ex-votos in thanksgiving for graces received.

itens.titulo: Shrine of Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré
itens.resumo: One of the largest Catholic shrines in North America, built by French sailors grateful to Saint Anne for saving them from a shipwreck in the 17th century.
itens.corpo:
The devotion began in 1658, when French sailors, grateful for having escaped a shipwreck on the Saint Lawrence River, built a first chapel dedicated to Saint Anne at the place called Petit Cap, today Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré, near Quebec City. Shortly afterward, in 1661, the first healing attributed to the saint's intercession was recorded there, in favor of the settler Louis Guimond, beginning centuries of pilgrimages.

The present basilica, in the Neo-Romanesque style, is the fifth church built on the site since the 17th century; its construction began in 1923 and it was consecrated by Cardinal Maurice Roy in 1976. Civil and ecclesiastical patroness of Quebec, Saint Anne is celebrated with a great annual pilgrimage on July 26, when the shrine receives the culmination of its novena and consolidates its place as one of the main Catholic pilgrimage destinations in North America.
itens.ano: parish founded in 1657; present basilica consecrated in 1976

itens.titulo: Basilica of the Santo Niño de Cebu
itens.resumo: The oldest church in the Philippines, built on the site where the first Spanish colonizers found intact, in 1565, the image of the Child Jesus left by Ferdinand Magellan decades earlier.
itens.corpo:
According to tradition, the image of the Santo Niño (Child Jesus) was given in 1521 by the Portuguese navigator Ferdinand Magellan to the local queen of Cebu on the occasion of her baptism, during the first circumnavigation of the globe. When the expedition of Miguel López de Legazpi returned to the island in 1565, under Spanish command, a soldier found the small wooden image intact amid the ashes of a burned village — an episode interpreted as a miracle, which led to the founding, on the same site, of the Augustinian church and convent that would become the Basilica of the Santo Niño, the oldest church in the Philippines.

On the occasion of the fourth centenary of the Christianization of the archipelago, Pope Paul VI raised the church to the rank of minor basilica in 1965. In 2013 an earthquake of magnitude 7.2 seriously damaged part of the structure, including its bell tower, but the basilica was restored and remains the main center of devotion to the Santo Niño, whose feast in January (the Sinulog) gathers millions of faithful in Cebu.

itens.titulo: Basilica of Our Lady of Good Health of Vailankanni
itens.resumo: Marian shrine in southern India, known as “the Lourdes of the East,” built around Marian apparitions reported in the sixteenth century.
itens.corpo:
Tradition places the origin of the devotion in Vailankanni, on the coast of Tamil Nadu, in two episodes of the sixteenth century: around 1570, a beautiful lady with a child in her arms is said to have asked a young shepherd boy, who was delivering milk around the region, for milk; and, around 1587, a crippled buttermilk seller is said to have received a similar request from a lady, who afterward told him to ask for a chapel to be built in her honor at a nearby site. To these two apparitions is added a third founding event, the rescue of Portuguese sailors from a storm at sea, attributed to the intercession of Our Lady.

Starting from a thatched chapel built in the mid-sixteenth century, the shrine grew over the centuries until it became a parish in 1771, during a period of persecution of Catholics under Dutch rule in the region. In 1962 Pope John XXIII granted it the title of minor basilica. Today the church, of Gothic architecture, attracts about five million pilgrims a year, among Catholics, Hindus and followers of other traditions, in one of the greatest phenomena of popular Marian devotion in Asia.
itens.ano: apparitions in the sixteenth century; minor basilica in 1962
